prerequisites.meaning: A unit processed or generated by a model; a text token can be a word, word part or character.
prerequisites.answer: No. A token can be a whole word, part of a word or punctuation.

prerequisites.meaning: A named piece of code taking inputs and returning an output.
prerequisites.answer: Inputs: the messages and settings such as max_tokens. Output: the generated reply.

prerequisites.meaning: A structured text format for exchanging fields and values, including objects and lists.
prerequisites.answer: max_tokens is the field name; 64 is its value.

prerequisites.meaning: An interface through which one program asks another to do work.
prerequisites.check: Does a browser need the provider's secret key?
prerequisites.answer: No. The secret key stays on the server; the browser talks to your server.

prerequisites.meaning: The elapsed time from a request to its result; first-token latency measures the initial wait.
prerequisites.check: Is first-token wait the same as full-answer wait?
prerequisites.answer: No. The first token usually arrives well before the full answer is finished.

diagrams.title: Checked Python request route
diagrams.subtitle: Allowed or blocked
trace: A fictional current message enters respond.
Input checks allow, redact or block the current message.
Allowed requests generate and check an answer; a blocked request takes the refusal branch.
Both paths record metadata without raw prompts.
diagrams.explanation: The core calls respond directly. Optional Gradio calls the same handler; it does not call FastAPI. Allowed current text enters generation and output checking. A blocked current message skips generation and sends a refusal to the logging/return step. Both branches log metadata. Earlier history is not automatically cleaned, and these limited rules miss other attacks. A public endpoint requires its own separate safeguards.
diagrams.check_answer: No. It goes straight to refusal and metadata logging.
diagrams.notes:
In short: The checked Python route blocks or cleans current input before fixed-weight generation and metadata logging.

Explain: The current request contains invented text and optional earlier history. The input rule checks length and a limited set of patterns. Allowed text reaches fixed-weight generation, followed by an output rule. Blocked input skips the model and receives a refusal. Both branches write metadata, while the separate API route needs its own controls.

Example: Call respond with a normal question and a literal injection phrase. The normal path records input and completion tokens. The blocked path records zero model tokens. The solid refusal branch goes directly from input checking to logging; it does not pass through generation.

Ask: Does a blocked current request reach generate?

Answer: No. It takes the refusal branch and is logged without a model call.

Watch out: Cleaning only the newest message does not clean old history, and pattern rules can miss paraphrased attacks.

diagrams.title: JSON request to continuation
diagrams.subtitle: In-process endpoint
trace: TestClient submits fictional JSON without a network port.
ChatRequest validates message roles and supported limits.
The template produces [1,L] input IDs; fixed weights generate up to 24 new IDs.
Slicing decodes only continuation tokens and returns separate usage counts.
diagrams.explanation: An endpoint maps a declared request to a Python handler. TestClient calls it within the notebook process. ChatRequest checks roles, text and supported output limits. Generate applies the model chat template, runs fixed weights under the lock, slices the input prefix and returns text plus counts. Invalid fields receive HTTP 422. This route is separate from respond, so it has no inherited pattern checks or production authentication.
diagrams.check_answer: The output contains input IDs plus continuation; only the continuation is the answer.
diagrams.notes:
In short: FastAPI transforms validated JSON messages into tokens, then returns continuation text and token counts.

Explain: JSON stores named request fields in structured text. Validation checks the roles, text and supported token limits. The chat template adds the model's expected role markers. Generation returns input IDs plus newly predicted IDs. Slicing removes the input prefix before decoding the assistant reply into text.

Example: An input has shape [1,L], meaning one sequence of L tokens. After at most 24 new tokens, output shape is [1,L+n]. Decode only the n continuation IDs. TestClient sends this request inside the process and does not measure real network travel.

Ask: Why remove the prefix before decoding the answer?

Answer: The full model output includes the question and role markers as well as its continuation.

Watch out: The small compatible schema has no production authentication and does not inherit the separate respond handler's guardrails.

diagrams.title: Four-request monitoring experiment
diagrams.subtitle: Other experiments separate
trace: Send four fictional requests through respond.
Record timing, tokens, model version and block reason without raw text.
Read all rows for request, blocking and redaction counts.
Filter allowed rows for latency percentiles; the tiny sample is illustrative.
diagrams.explanation: This diagram describes only the coherent monitoring experiment. Stream timing, FastAPI tests, cost arithmetic, rounding/PPL, batching and caching are independent exercises. Four invented requests pass through respond, creating metadata-only log rows. Monitoring reads those rows. Total, blocked and redacted counts use the full table; latency percentiles use only allowed rows. A four-request p95 illustrates aggregation but is not a stable service guarantee.
diagrams.check_answer: No. Only allowed-request latencies enter that percentile.
diagrams.notes:
In short: Follow the four-request monitoring experiment rather than falsely connecting independent lab exercises.

Explain: Synthetic traffic means invented requests used to inspect application behaviour. The respond handler applies limited checks and records metadata for each request. The log becomes a table for analysis. Filtering separates allowed requests for latency percentiles. Block and redaction counts still use the complete traffic table.

Example: The bounded core sends four fictional messages: ordinary, unsupported factual, blocked and redacted. Count all four rows, then compute percentiles only from allowed rows. Streaming, cost arithmetic, quantisation, batching and endpoint testing are separate exercises, not inputs to this monitoring pipeline.

Ask: Do blocked rows enter the allowed-request latency percentile?

Answer: No. They remain in total-request and blocking counts but are excluded from that latency population.

Watch out: Four examples demonstrate aggregation; their p95 value is unstable and cannot establish a production service guarantee.

diagrams.title: Round and reconstruct weights
diagrams.subtitle: Precision probe; no training
diagrams.explanation: This diagram follows fake_quantize and the numerical error calculation. The input weights are reshaped into groups. Each group produces one scale from its largest absolute value divided by the permitted integer maximum. The arrows carry group values together with their scales into rounding. Original groups travel alongside the integers for the final error comparison. Reconstructed weights remain floating point, and the layer-error dictionary compares them with the originals. Full-model perplexity scoring and restoration are separate steps described in the lab; this diagram does not train weights or show packed integer storage.
trace: Reshape the selected weight matrix into rows or groups; M counts groups and g their size.
Compute each scale from its largest magnitude divided by qmax, using a floor for zero groups.
Divide group values by their scales, round and clamp to the permitted integer range.
Multiply integers by the same scales to reconstruct floating-point weights, then measure relative error.
Full-model PPL scoring and finally restoration are separate uses of this helper in the lab.
diagrams.check_answer: No. They are temporarily approximated and then restored.
diagrams.notes:
In short: Fake quantisation groups weights, computes scales, rounds values and reconstructs floating-point approximations.

Explain: Reshaping creates M groups of g values without changing the underlying numbers. Each group gets a scale from its largest magnitude and chosen integer range. Rounding divides the original group values by that scale before choosing integers. Reconstruction multiplies those integers by the same scale. Relative error compares reconstructed weights with the original values; this is measurement, not training.

Example: With four bits and group maximum one, qmax is seven and the scale is one divided by seven. A value of 0.2 becomes integer one, then reconstructs to approximately 0.143. Labelled bundles carry original groups, scales and integer codes through the operations without changing the original groups.

Ask: Are reconstructed tensors stored as packed four-bit integers?

Answer: No. They remain floating point; the separate size estimate describes hypothetical packed storage.

Watch out: Scoring perplexity and restoring full-model weights are separate lab operations, outside this helper diagram.

diagrams.title: Response cache hit or miss
diagrams.subtitle: Same request identity
diagrams.explanation: Cached generation reuses a completed answer for the same declared request. The key covers model identity, messages and output cap. A hit returns stored text without another model call. A miss generates then stores a reply. The library-hours example has no attached timetable, so a cached answer can remain unsupported. Prefix caching is a different operation that reuses input computation.
trace: Hash the model identity, complete messages and output cap.
Look up that exact identity in CACHE.
A miss generates and stores text; a hit jumps directly to the stored answer.
Change one field to make a new key; check answer evidence independently.
diagrams.check_answer: No. Only the miss branch generates.
diagrams.notes:
In short: A response cache reuses a completed answer only for the same model, messages and output limit.

Explain: The request fields define the operation to repeat. A hash turns those fields into a dictionary key. A cache lookup either finds an answer or misses. Only a miss reaches fixed-weight generation before storing the reply. A hit takes a direct branch to the reused answer without another model call.

Example: Call the same invented library-hours request twice with the same cap. The first call generates and the second retrieves stored text. Change the cap or messages to create a new key. Both replies still lack a timetable source, so neither caching nor generation establishes correct opening hours.

Ask: Does the hit branch perform generation again?

Answer: No. It returns the existing answer; generation is needed only for a miss.

Watch out: Cache identity and freshness must cover relevant settings, and cached unsupported answers remain unsupported.

glossary.meaning: A URL and request handler through which a program exposes an operation.
The elapsed time from a request to its result; first-token latency measures the initial wait.
Work completed per unit time, such as total generated tokens per second.
Time to first token; this lab approximates it with first non-empty decoded text.
Representing weights with a limited set of values, often to store fewer bits.
Processing several inputs together in one model operation.
Stored results reused when an equivalent request returns.
A latency value at or below which roughly 95% of measured requests fall.
A measurement including specified initialisation work; state which downloads or setup it includes.
The response used here when request validation fails before generation.
Saved complete answers reused only when all response-changing inputs match.
Invented requests used to exercise an application and its monitoring.
An in-process HTTP request tester; its timing excludes real network transport.
A measurement after specified initialisation or warm-up; state what work it excludes.

pitfalls: Higher batching throughput does not automatically mean lower latency for every individual user.
The notebook's fake quantisation size estimates do not describe actual packed tensor memory.
The Gradio path and FastAPI path are separate exercises; input checks in respond do not protect the API endpoint.

recap.title: Week 11: operate an application
recap.question: More throughput: always shorter waits?
recap.answer: No. Aggregate work can rise while individual requests wait longer.
recap.notes:
In short: Operate the whole request path and justify decisions using quality, timing, cost and data evidence.

Explain: The model, runtime, coordination and interface have different responsibilities. API contracts describe fields rather than identical model behaviour. Efficiency changes require quality checks as well as speed measurements. Packaging records tested versions, while monitoring records operational behaviour. Every reachable route needs its own validated controls and failure handling.

Example: Return to the fictional 500-student assistant. State its expected traffic, data location and quality target before choosing deployment. Then inspect first text, full wait, throughput, token costs and failures. A modest working demo is useful evidence, but it is not a capacity or safety guarantee.

Ask: If batching doubles throughput, must every student wait less?

Answer: No. Aggregate work can rise while individual requests wait longer for batching or shared capacity.

Watch out: Keep archived measurements labelled and replace them only through a measured export, results comparison and the fill pipeline.

vocabulary_notes:
In short: Read tokens, APIs and latency as different parts of one application request.

Explain: A token is a unit processed by the language model. An API is an interface through which programs request work. JSON expresses named fields in structured text. Latency is the elapsed wait for a request. The same request may contain many tokens, and its latency includes more than token generation.

Example: An invented JSON request contains one user message and max_tokens=24. The tokenizer may split a word into several IDs before the model runs. The client receives text and usage fields after a measurable wait. Field validity does not establish answer correctness or actual network capacity.

Ask: Are characters, tokens and latency interchangeable measurements?

Answer: No. They measure text symbols, model processing units and elapsed time respectively.

Watch out: First decoded text is an approximate token timestamp; do not describe an in-process TestClient duration as network latency.
